prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: After, Elinor, Lipper

outputs.L1:
**After Elinor Lipper**

The creature that had once been a man  
handed his lord and master  
his petition—a stained and grimy scrap—  
asking to be transferred  
to the status of a horse.

“You son of a whore,” the master bellowed,  
kicking him for good measure.  
“What do you mean by this?”

The creature that had once been a man,  
having considered his petition deeply,  
answered:

“If I were a horse, I would have  
one day off in ten. As it is,  
I have none. As a horse,  
I could rest now and again  
during work. As a former man,  
I cannot.

“As a horse, I would be expected  
to perform work equal to my strength.  
As a prisoner, I am always hungry,  
and, hungry, I work less  
and receive less bread,  
so I can barely stand.

“A horse gets a stable  
and two blankets. I have  
no blankets, no jacket.

“If a driver beats  
a horse too hard, he is punished,  
for a horse is precious.  
If the brigadiers beat and kick me,  
it is like beating a tree.

“So you see,  
a prisoner is nothing here.  
But a horse?  
A horse is something!”

Within the frozen  
and broken vista, the plea  
had a ring of truth, heard even  
by the lord and master,  
who had once been a man himself  
and who, when no other former men could see,  
attached that name to the page, granting  
the horse a stable and two blankets.
outputs.L2:
**After Elinor Lipper**

The being who had once been human brought his ruler a filthy, discolored piece of paper. On it, he requested that he be reclassified as a horse.

His master struck him with a boot and roared, “You bastard—what is this supposed to mean?”

The former man had thought carefully about his appeal. He explained that a horse was allowed one free day out of every ten, while he received no days off at all. A horse could pause occasionally while laboring; he, as someone stripped of his humanity, could not. A horse was required to do only as much as its physical power permitted. A prisoner, however, was kept constantly hungry. Hunger reduced his ability to work, and reduced work brought smaller bread rations, leaving him scarcely able to remain upright.

A horse was given shelter in a stable and provided with two blankets. He possessed neither blankets nor even a jacket. If a driver used excessive force against a horse, the driver faced punishment because the animal had value. But when brigadiers punched and kicked him, it mattered no more than striking a tree.

That, he said, was the difference: in this place, a prisoner counted for nothing, whereas a horse counted for something.

Amid the ruined, icebound landscape, the argument sounded true even to the master—a man who had also once been human. Later, when none of the other former men were watching, he signed his name to the petition and approved the requested change, awarding the new horse a stable and two blankets.
outputs.L3:
A prisoner, stripped of dignity and treated as less than human, petitions his master for an extraordinary favor: he asks to be granted the status of a horse. His request is not intended as a joke. Rather, it exposes the profound cruelty of a system in which an animal’s welfare is valued more highly than a human life.

In support of his plea, the prisoner explains that a horse is occasionally allowed to rest and is assigned work according to its strength. Prisoners, by contrast, are driven relentlessly, with little regard for exhaustion, illness, or physical limits. He also observes that horses receive adequate food and shelter. They are kept in stables and provided with blankets, while prisoners are often left starving, inadequately clothed, and exposed to harsh conditions.

The prisoner further argues that a horse is protected from excessive beatings because it is considered valuable property. A master knows that severe mistreatment might weaken or destroy the animal and diminish its usefulness. Prisoners, however, are treated as though they possess no value at all and may therefore be abused without restraint or concern.

The master recognizes the painful truth of this reasoning. Though unwilling to acknowledge it openly, he secretly approves the prisoner’s request. He grants the man a place in the stable and provides him with two blankets—offering him, under the status of an animal, the basic care and protection that had been denied to him as a human being.
outputs.L4:
Every morning before dawn, the prisoners were driven from the barracks into the yard. They stood barefoot in mud or frost while the overseers counted them, struck them, and counted them again. By the time the sun rose, each man had ceased to be a name. He was a number, a pair of hands, a back expected to bend until it broke.

One prisoner, known only as Forty-Seven, worked in the master’s stables. He hauled water, forked manure, polished harnesses, and carried sacks of grain he was forbidden to taste. The horses slept on clean straw beneath a sound roof. They were brushed each evening, blanketed in winter, and examined whenever they limped or refused their feed. No one beat them without reason. A bruised horse lost value, and the master guarded his property carefully.

Forty-Seven watched and learned.

For three days he composed a petition in his mind. On the fourth, he stole a scrap of paper from the clerk’s room and made ink from soot and water. He wrote slowly, shaping the letters with a splinter of wood.

“To the Master,” the petition began. “I request that I no longer be classified as a prisoner. I ask instead to be entered in your records as a horse.”

The master read the petition at supper. At first he laughed so loudly that the servants paused outside the dining room.

“A horse?” he said when Forty-Seven was dragged before him. “Have you lost what remains of your mind?”

“No, Master.”

“Then explain yourself.”

Forty-Seven kept his eyes lowered. “A horse is allowed to rest after labor, because exhaustion reduces its usefulness. A horse is given sufficient food, because hunger weakens it. A horse is sheltered from rain and frost, because sickness is expensive. If a horse is injured, its wound is cleaned. If someone beats a horse too severely, he is punished for damaging the master’s property.”

The servants stared at the floor. The overseer’s hand tightened around his whip.

“And you believe you deserve these things?” the master asked.

Forty-Seven shook his head. “Deserving has nothing to do with it. I ask only to be valued.”

The room became still.

The master looked at the prisoner’s body: the ribs visible beneath torn cloth, the infected cut on one shoulder, the swollen feet, the scar above his eye. None of these injuries had troubled him before. Prisoners were plentiful. Their suffering cost nothing.

But the petition had placed a price upon that suffering.

“If I were listed as a horse,” Forty-Seven continued, “I would not ask to be free. I would pull carts, carry loads, and obey commands. I would ask only for the care given to an animal whose labor you wish to preserve.”

The overseer stepped forward. “Master, let me punish him. This mockery will spread.”

“No,” said the master.

He read the petition again. Its reasoning was insolent, yet flawless. To deny it, he would have to admit openly that he treated men worse than beasts. To grant it publicly would be more dangerous still, for the other prisoners might discover that the rules of property offered more protection than the rules of humanity.

“Take him away,” the master ordered. “Say nothing of this.”

That night he summoned the clerk.

In a locked ledger kept apart from the plantation accounts, the clerk crossed out Forty-Seven’s number and entered a new designation: *stable horse, dark coat, age uncertain*. The change was never announced. No one was to speak of it.

From then on, Forty-Seven received a bowl of oats with his evening ration. He was allowed to sleep in the stable on clean straw. When fever took him, the veterinarian was called. The overseer was forbidden to strike him above the legs or across the back. After long journeys, he was given water before being assigned another task.

The other prisoners noticed the change but did not understand it. Some thought Forty-Seven had become an informer. Others believed the master had developed an eccentric affection for him. Forty-Seven offered no explanation. He carried harnesses, cleaned stalls, and accepted each small mercy with the silence expected of livestock.

The master also remained silent. Yet whenever he visited the stable, he avoided Forty-Seven’s eyes. He could no longer pretend that cruelty was merely order, or that ownership relieved him of moral responsibility. The prisoner’s petition had forced him to recognize a truth he had spent years denying: in his world, a man had to surrender his humanity before he could receive humane treatment.

Forty-Seven survived, but survival came at a terrible price. To be fed, he had to be called an animal. To be protected, he had to become property worth preserving. His secret reclassification did not restore his dignity; it proved how completely dignity had been excluded from the system.

And the master, though still obeyed and feared, was diminished as well. He had accepted the argument because he understood it. He knew that the stable contained more mercy than the barracks, and that his animals lived under kinder laws than the people he ruled.

Thus the petition was granted, and both men were condemned by it: the prisoner to live as a horse, and the master to know that he had ceased to behave as a man.
outputs.L5:
### After

After the storm, Elinor found a small wooden box washed onto the riverbank. The brass plate on its lid bore a single name: **Lipper**.

Inside lay a silver compass, though its needle pointed neither north nor south. Instead, it turned slowly toward the ruined lighthouse beyond the cliffs.

Elinor followed.

At the lighthouse door, the compass stopped. Carved into the weathered wood were the words: *What is lost does not always wish to be found.*

She hesitated, listening to the waves below. Then she slipped the compass into her pocket and walked home.

Some mysteries, Elinor decided, were more powerful when left unopened.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem inspired by Elinor Lipper about a starving labor-camp prisoner who petitions to be treated as a horse because horses receive better food, rest, shelter, and protection.
counterfactuals.output:
### Petition to the Commandant

I request reassignment  
from the species *man*  
to the species *horse*.

A horse receives oats,  
measured but real.  
Its water is not soup  
remembering a cabbage.

A horse is rested  
before it falls.  
Its wounds are washed  
because leather and bone  
belong to the State.

A horse has a roof  
without holes cut for stars,  
straw not stolen from its breath,  
a blanket permitted  
to remain a blanket.

No guard strikes a horse  
for walking slowly  
when the road is ice.  
No overseer asks a horse  
to confess that hunger  
is sabotage.

A horse may be thin,  
but not uselessly thin.  
Men calculate its ribs  
with concern.

Therefore I ask  
for four legs in the ledger,  
a mane in the inventory,  
iron shoes, a stall,  
and the small protection  
granted to valuable things.

I will pull whatever you harness to me.  
I will learn the dumb patience  
you already require.

Only feed me  
as you feed the animals.

Only let me sleep  
where the animals sleep.

Only call me beast—

and mean by it  
something worth keeping alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a bleak prose poem titled “After Elinor Lipper” in which a dehumanized prisoner asks his brutal master to transfer him to the status of a horse.
counterfactuals.output:
# After Elinor Lipper

At dawn the horses received oats. Steam rose from their backs like the last warmth leaving a house. A man stood beside them, numbered, hollowed by winter, his hands no longer persuaded they belonged to him.

When the master came with his whip and polished boots, the man lowered his eyes.

“Transfer me,” he said.

The master laughed. “To which barrack?”

“To the horses.”

The whip lifted his chin.

“I can pull,” the man continued. “I can sleep standing. I will not ask where the others have gone. Brand me. Harness me. Only give me their ration, their blanket, the hand that checks for wounds.”

The horses shifted, troubled by his voice.

The master struck him for confusing the order of creation.

All day the man hauled stones through the snow. At evening, one horse stumbled. Six prisoners were ordered to raise it. The master cursed them gently, almost tenderly, for letting the animal suffer.

That night, beneath a sky as hard as the frozen trough, the man practiced forgetting his name. By morning he could remember only the word *horse*, and even that was too human a hope.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Turn an account of Gulag conditions into a literary poem: have a prisoner explain that a horse gets days off, blankets, adequate food, and protection from beatings, while prisoners get nothing.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Horse**

The horse has Sundays.  
They loosen the harness,  
rub frost from its flanks,  
lay a blanket over its steam.

The horse has oats measured  
into a wooden trough,  
hay enough to keep  
the ribs from showing.

No guard may strike it—  
not without cause, they say;  
the animal is valuable,  
the animal must last.

But we are given no Sunday.  
The cold lies down with us.  
Our bowls shine through their soup.  
Our bones count themselves.

A man may beat us  
until the stick grows tired.  
No one asks what we are worth.

So when the horse passes,  
warm beneath its blanket,  
I do not envy its freedom.

I envy that someone  
has decided  
it must live.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark, surreal narrative poem about a man reduced to a “creature” who submits a stained petition to become a horse, ending with his overseer secretly granting the request.
counterfactuals.output:
### The Petition of Hooves

They had stopped calling him a man  
after the winter of the black alarms.  
In ledgers he was *creature*:  
one ration, one shovel,  
one mouth permitted to open  
only for orders.

He slept beneath the sorting house  
where pipes dreamed rust into buckets  
and the walls perspired fingerprints.  
Each morning the overseer counted him  
with the broken tools.

Still, the creature remembered horses—  
their dark, ungovernable eyes,  
the thunder folded in their knees,  
the mercy of a body  
made only to run or be ruined.

So he wrote a petition.

He wrote it on a flour sack  
with a nail dipped in lampblack,  
then signed it with the blood  
that leaked from his left boot.

> I request four legs.  
> I request the abolition of speech.  
> I request a mane against the weather.  
> Let the bit replace my name.  
> Let the road judge me.

The petition bore other stains:  
soup, rain, rat tracks,  
a yellow bloom from the infirmary wall.  
He pressed it through the brass slot  
marked **APPEALS / CONFESSIONS / WASTE**  
and waited.

Days passed like carts of bones.

The clerks laughed until their teeth  
clicked loose in their mouths.  
They stamped **IMPOSSIBLE** across the page,  
then **INSOLENT**, then **RETURN TO LABOR**.  
The overseer said nothing.

That night, beneath a moon  
thin as a butcher’s hook,  
he came alone to the creature’s stall.  
He locked the yard.  
He shuttered the watchtowers.  
From his coat he drew the stained petition,  
folded small as a dead bird.

“You understand,” he whispered,  
“this must never be entered.”

Then he touched the creature’s spine.

Bone lengthened with a sound  
like frozen branches breaking.  
Hands blackened into hooves.  
The jaw pushed forward, mercifully  
beyond language. A mane spilled out,  
coarse and midnight-blue.

Before dawn, a horse stood trembling  
where the creature had knelt.

The overseer opened the final gate  
and struck no bell.

In the official ledger he wrote:  
**CREATURE—MISSING.  
REQUEST—DENIED.**

But far beyond the sorting house,  
the earth shook softly under hooves,  
and the overseer, hiding his smile,  
burned the petition for warmth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an emotionally restrained free-verse piece exploring dehumanization in a frozen prison camp, contrasting the value placed on working animals with the worthlessness assigned to human prisoners.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn the horses are counted first.

Steam lifts from their backs  
as if the cold has granted them  
a private weather.

Their oats are measured.  
A man checks each hoof for ice,  
runs a careful hand along the fetlock,  
notes the beginning of a sore.

A lame horse cannot haul timber.  
A dead horse must be replaced.

Beyond the stable, prisoners wait  
in rows that lose their edges  
to the snow.

No one asks where their boots leak.  
No one records the cough  
that passed through the barracks  
and settled in their lungs.

They are counted also,  
but differently—

not as bodies requiring shelter,  
not as lives,

only as numbers that should still move  
when the gate opens.

All day the horses drag the sledges.  
All day the men load them.

When an animal stumbles,  
the column stops.

When a prisoner falls,  
the column closes  
over the space.

At evening the horses are rubbed down.  
Blankets are brought.  
Water is warmed enough  
not to crack their teeth.

The prisoners stand beneath the searchlight,  
snow gathering on their shoulders.

One horse turns its dark eye  
toward them.

No mercy in it.  
No cruelty.

Only the calm regard  
of something whose suffering  
has a price.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
